questions.title: WIMP
questions.text:
A graphical user interface is often called a WIMP interface. Complete the words.

W = [[1]], I = [[2]], M = [[3]], P = [[4]]

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) windows (2) icons (3) menus (4) pointer

questions.title: Types of interface
questions.text: Match each type of user interface to its description.

right.text: The user types exact commands at a prompt
The user clicks icons, windows and menus with a pointer
The user speaks or types ordinary sentences
The user's hand or body movements are detected by sensors

scheme.mark_scheme: CLI–R1, GUI–R2, NLI–R3, GRI–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: CLI and memory
questions.text: A command line interface needs more memory and processing power than a graphical user interface.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A CLI shows only text, so it uses far fewer resources than a GUI, which must draw windows, icons and graphics.

questions.title: Advantages of a GUI
questions.text: State **two** advantages of a graphical user interface.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): easy to learn / intuitive; no need to remember commands — icons are recognised; suitable for beginners / non-technical users; fewer errors because options are selected; WYSIWYG — see the result; easy multitasking with several windows / drag and drop; can display images and video; consistent layout between programs
scheme.model_answer: 1 Users do not need to remember commands because they can click on icons. 2 Several programs can be open in separate windows at the same time.
scheme.ai_instructions: 'Easy to use' and 'user-friendly' count as the same point.

questions.title: Disadvantage of a GUI
questions.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of a graphical user interface.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Disadvantage (1) + explanation (1), e.g.
- Uses a lot of memory / processing power / storage (1) because it has to draw graphics, icons and windows (1)
- Slower for expert users (1) because many clicks / menus are needed for a task that one command could do (1)
- Hard to automate repetitive tasks (1) so the same clicks must be repeated (1)
- Some advanced settings are hidden (1) so users have less control (1)
scheme.model_answer: It uses a lot of memory and processing power, because it has to display windows, icons and other graphics all the time.

questions.title: Advantages of a CLI
questions.text: State **two** advantages of a command line interface.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): faster for expert users / one command does a lot; full / direct control over the OS / all settings; uses little memory / processing power; tasks can be automated with scripts; works well for remote access / low bandwidth
scheme.model_answer: 1 An expert can complete tasks faster by typing one command. 2 It uses very little memory and processing power.

questions.title: Disadvantage of a CLI
questions.text: Explain why a command line interface is **not** suitable for a beginner.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): the user must remember / learn many commands; commands must be typed with exact syntax; typing errors cause error messages / unwanted actions (e.g. deleting files); not intuitive / no visual clues; error messages are hard to understand
scheme.model_answer: A beginner would have to remember many commands and type them with exactly the right syntax, and a small typing mistake could cause an error or even delete the wrong files.

questions.title: GUI or CLI
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement applies to a **GUI** or a **CLI**.

prefill: Commands must be remembered and typed exactly
Suitable for users with no training
Repetitive tasks can easily be automated with scripts
Needs more memory and processing power
Uses icons that the user recognises
Works well on a server accessed over a slow network

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 CLI; 2 GUI; 3 CLI; 4 GUI; 5 GUI; 6 CLI

Six correct (4); five (3); three or four (2); one or two (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award 4 for six correct rows, 3 for five, 2 for three or four, 1 for one or two.

questions.title: Compare GUI and CLI
questions.text: Compare a graphical user interface with a command line interface.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides needed: GUI easy to learn / intuitive vs CLI commands must be remembered; GUI uses more memory / CPU vs CLI few resources; CLI faster for experts vs GUI slower (many clicks); CLI gives full control / scripting vs GUI limited to menus; GUI fewer errors vs CLI typing errors; GUI shows graphics vs CLI text only
scheme.model_answer: A GUI is easier to learn because users click icons and menus, whereas a CLI requires users to remember exact commands. However, a GUI uses much more memory and processing power than a CLI.
scheme.ai_instructions: A point about only one interface, with no comparison, gets no mark.

questions.title: Recognising a CLI
questions.text: A technician types `copy *.docx D:\backup` and presses Enter. Which type of interface is being used?

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: An exact command with syntax typed at a prompt is a CLI.

questions.title: Choose the interface
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the **most suitable** interface.

prefill: A driver wants to make a phone call while driving
A network administrator configures 40 servers with a script
A surgeon needs to scroll through X-rays without touching anything
A grandmother uses a tablet to look at family photos

scheme.mark_scheme: Driver → Natural language (1); Administrator → CLI (1); Surgeon → Gesture (1); Grandmother → GUI (1)

questions.title: Natural language interface
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **natural language interface**, and give **one** example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The user communicates with the computer using ordinary human language, spoken or typed (1)
- Example: Siri / Alexa / Google Assistant / chatbot / voice control in a car (1)

points.criterion: Ordinary human language, spoken or typed

scheme.model_answer: The user gives instructions in ordinary spoken or typed language instead of commands, for example asking Siri to set an alarm.

questions.title: How a voice assistant understands
questions.text: Describe how a voice assistant processes the spoken request "Set an alarm for seven o'clock".

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three (1 each):
- A microphone captures the sound (and it is digitised)
- Speech recognition converts the speech into text
- Natural language processing analyses the words / grammar to find the meaning / intent (set alarm, 7:00)
- The device carries out the action
- It replies using speech synthesis / text-to-speech
scheme.model_answer: The microphone records the voice, speech recognition turns the sound into text, and natural language processing works out that the user wants an alarm at 7:00. The assistant sets the alarm and confirms it using speech synthesis.

questions.title: Advantages of NLI
questions.text: Select **two** advantages of a natural language interface.

options.content: It is never affected by background noise
Users do not need to learn special commands

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Background noise and accents are typical problems for NLIs.

questions.title: Disadvantages of NLI
questions.text: State **two** disadvantages of a natural language interface.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): language is ambiguous / misinterpretation; struggles with colloquial language, homophones, context; accents / dialects / speech impairments; background noise; users may need to learn specific phrases; limited languages supported; privacy — always listening / recordings stored; needs processing power / Internet
scheme.model_answer: 1 Human language is ambiguous, so the system may misunderstand the request. 2 It may not recognise the words if there is background noise or a strong accent.

questions.title: NLI and homophones
questions.text: A natural language interface may confuse words that sound the same, such as "write" and "right".

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Homophones are a source of ambiguity; the system must use context to decide which word was meant.

questions.title: Gesture recognition interface
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **gesture recognition interface**, and give **one** example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Movements of the user's hands / body are detected by sensors / cameras / touchscreen and interpreted as commands (1)
- Example: swipe / pinch-to-zoom on a phone; Kinect; waving to control a smart TV; VR controllers (1)

points.criterion: Body movements detected and interpreted as commands

scheme.model_answer: An interface in which sensors such as cameras or a touchscreen detect the user's hand or body movements and interpret them as commands, for example pinching to zoom on a phone.

questions.title: Gesture input
questions.text: Select **two** examples of a gesture recognition interface.

options.content: Swiping left on a phone screen to see the next photo
Waving a hand in front of a games console camera to pause a game
Asking a smart speaker for the weather

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Gesture: advantage and disadvantage
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of a gesture recognition interface.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): natural / intuitive; touchless — hygienic; useful for people who cannot use a keyboard / mouse; immersive for games / VR; frees the hands

Disadvantage (1): gestures misinterpreted / accidental gestures; users must learn gestures; limited number of commands; tiring; expensive sensors; affected by lighting / space; less precise
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: the user can control the device without touching it. Disadvantage: an accidental movement may be read as a command.

questions.title: One disadvantage of each
questions.text: Write **one** disadvantage of each of the following user interfaces.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Natural language (1): ambiguous, leading to misinterpretation of user input; system may struggle with colloquial language, homophones or context; users may need to learn specific phrases; accents / background noise; privacy

Gesture recognition (1): gestures may be misinterpreted / unintended commands; users must learn the gestures; limited set of commands; tiring; needs cameras / sensors; affected by lighting
scheme.model_answer: Natural language: the system may misinterpret the user because language is ambiguous. Gesture recognition: an accidental movement may be recognised as a command.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each box is marked separately; the disadvantage must belong to that interface.

questions.title: Interfaces in a restaurant kitchen
questions.text:
Chefs in a busy restaurant kitchen need to look up recipes on a screen while their hands are covered in flour or oil. The kitchen is noisy.

Discuss whether a **natural language interface** or a **gesture recognition interface** would be more suitable. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Both are touchless, so the screen stays clean / chefs do not need to wash hands (1)
- NLI: hands-free and no gestures to learn (1), but the noisy kitchen makes speech recognition unreliable / misinterpretation (1)
- GRI: works in a noisy kitchen (1), but gestures may be misread / need to be learnt / steam or lighting may affect the camera (1)
- Justified conclusion, e.g. gesture because of the noise (1)

points.criterion: Valid point about NLI linked to the kitchen
Valid point about GRI linked to the kitchen
A drawback of one of the interfaces in this setting

scheme.model_answer: Both interfaces let chefs use the screen without touching it, so it stays clean. A natural language interface would be hands-free, but the kitchen is noisy, so the system would often misunderstand the chefs. A gesture interface is not affected by noise; the chefs could swipe in the air to change page, although they would need to learn the gestures. Gesture recognition is more suitable because of the noise.
scheme.ai_instructions: Either choice can get full marks if justified using the scenario.

questions.title: Evaluate four interfaces
questions.text: A museum wants an interactive information point for visitors of all ages, including people with visual impairments. Evaluate the use of a **GUI**, a **CLI**, a **natural language interface** and a **gesture recognition interface** for this information point, and recommend the most suitable one(s).

scheme.mark_scheme:
Evaluation points (max 5), e.g.
- GUI: intuitive icons / touch, no training (1); but not usable by visually impaired visitors (1)
- CLI: unsuitable — visitors would need to know commands / not intuitive (1)
- NLI: visitors can ask questions in speech, good for visually impaired visitors / children (1); but noise in the museum / accents / language may cause misinterpretation (1)
- GRI: touchless, hygienic, engaging (1); but gestures must be learnt / limited commands / not accessible to all (1)

Recommendation justified (1), e.g. a touch GUI combined with a natural language (voice) option for visually impaired visitors

points.criterion: Further point linked to the visitors / museum

scheme.model_answer: A touch-screen GUI is intuitive for visitors of all ages because they just touch icons, but visually impaired visitors cannot see the icons. A CLI is unsuitable because visitors would have to know exact commands. A natural language interface lets visitors simply ask questions aloud, which helps visually impaired people and children, although noise in the museum and different accents may cause it to misunderstand. A gesture interface is engaging and touchless, but visitors would have to learn the gestures and it would not help blind visitors. I recommend a touch GUI with a voice (natural language) option, so that every visitor can use the information point.

summary: The advantages and disadvantages of graphical user interfaces (GUI), command line interfaces (CLI), natural language interfaces (NLI) and gesture recognition interfaces (GRI), and how to compare and choose between them.

blocks.content: The part of a computer system that lets the **user communicate with the computer**: how the user **gives instructions** (input) and how the computer **shows information and results** (output). It is usually provided by the operating system or the application.

A good interface is **easy to learn**, **efficient** to use, gives clear **feedback** and **prevents errors**. The best type depends on **who** the users are, **what** they do and **which device** they use.

flowchart LR
  UI[User interfaces] --> CLI[Command line interface]
  UI --> GUI[Graphical user interface]
  UI --> MENU[Menu-driven interface]
  UI --> NLI[Natural language interface]
  UI --> GRI[Gesture recognition interface]
blocks.caption: Main types of user interface

blocks.content: An interface in which the user **types commands** at a **prompt** using the keyboard; the computer executes each command and shows the result as **text**. Examples: Windows **Command Prompt / PowerShell**, the Linux / macOS **terminal (bash)**, router configuration consoles.

$ mkdir reports                 # create a folder
$ cp *.csv reports/             # copy every CSV file into it
$ ls -l reports                 # list the folder in detail
$ rm reports/old_*.csv          # delete all files whose names start with old_
blocks.caption: Commands typed in a Linux terminal

items.title: Advantages of a CLI
items.content:
- **Fast** for expert users — one typed command can do a lot of work (e.g. copy hundreds of files).
- Gives **direct, full control** over the OS, including settings not available in a GUI.
- Uses **little memory and processing power** — no graphics; works on old or low-powered computers and servers.
- Commands can be saved as **scripts** to **automate** repetitive tasks.
- Works well for **remote access** over slow network connections (e.g. SSH to a server).

items.title: Disadvantages of a CLI
items.content:
- **Hard to learn** — the user must **remember** commands and their exact syntax.
- **Easy to make errors** — a typing mistake gives an error or, worse, deletes the wrong files; often no undo.
- **Not intuitive** for beginners; little visual feedback.
- Text only — **unsuitable** for graphics, video or photo editing.
- Confusing error messages.

blocks.content: An interface in which the user interacts with **graphical objects** — **W**indows, **I**cons, **M**enus and a **P**ointer (**WIMP**) — by **pointing and clicking** with a mouse or **touching** a screen. Examples: Windows, macOS, Android, iOS.

blocks.title: The WIMP elements
rows: A rectangular area showing one program or document; can be moved, resized, minimised
A small picture representing a file, folder, program or action
A list of options to choose from (drop-down, pop-up, ribbon)
The arrow moved by a mouse / touchpad to select objects

items.title: Advantages of a GUI
items.content:
- **Easy to learn and use** — intuitive; users **recognise** icons instead of remembering commands.
- Suitable for **beginners and non-technical users**, children and the elderly.
- **Fewer errors** — users choose from options instead of typing commands; **undo** is usually available.
- **WYSIWYG** (what you see is what you get) — users see the result as they work.
- Easy **multitasking** — several windows can be open; drag-and-drop between them.
- Can display **graphics, images and video**; consistent layout between applications.

items.title: Disadvantages of a GUI
items.content:
- Uses **more memory, processing power and storage** than a CLI.
- Can be **slower for expert users** — many clicks through menus for one task.
- **Repetitive tasks** are harder to automate.
- Some advanced settings are **hidden** or not available.
- Needs a pointing device / touchscreen and a good display.

blocks.title: GUI vs CLI
rows: Points and clicks / touches icons, menus, windows
Types text commands at a prompt
**Faster** — one command can do a lot
Limited to what the menus offer

blocks.title: The same task in both interfaces — copy all photos into a new folder
blocks.content:
**GUI:** open File Explorer → right-click → *New folder* → type the name → select all photos with the mouse → drag them into the folder. Easy to see what is happening, but many steps.

**CLI:** `mkdir photos` then `cp *.jpg photos/` — two short commands, but the user must know them exactly.

blocks.title: Which interface?
rows: A primary-school pupil using a learning app
Intuitive icons; no commands to learn
A network administrator configuring 50 servers remotely
Fast, scripts can automate it, low bandwidth
An old computer with very little RAM
Needs to see and manipulate images
A ticket machine at a railway station
Limited set of options; no training needed

blocks.title: Menu-driven interfaces
blocks.content: A **menu-driven interface** presents a **series of menus** from which the user selects options (ATMs, ticket machines, a TV settings menu). It is very easy to use and prevents invalid choices, but it is **limited** to the options offered and can be **slow** if there are many levels of menus.

An interface that lets the user communicate with the computer in **ordinary human language** — **spoken** or **typed** — instead of commands or menus. Examples: voice assistants (**Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant**), chatbots, voice control in cars, voice search.

blocks.title: How a spoken NLI works
items: **Speech recognition** converts the sound of the voice into **text**.
**Natural language processing (NLP)** analyses the words and grammar to work out the **meaning / intent** ("set an alarm", "for 7 am").
The system carries out the request.
The reply is given as text or by **speech synthesis** (text-to-speech).

items.title: Advantages of an NLI
items.content:
- **No need to learn** commands — users speak or type naturally.
- **Hands-free** and eyes-free — useful while driving, cooking or for people with **physical or visual disabilities**.
- **Fast** for simple requests — speaking is quicker than typing.
- Suitable for people who **cannot read or type well** and for young children.
- Can be used on devices with **no keyboard or screen** (smart speakers).

items.title: Disadvantages of an NLI
items.content:
- Human language is **ambiguous** — the system may **misinterpret** the request (homophones, slang, context).
- Problems with **accents, dialects**, speech impairments and **background noise**.
- Users may need to learn **specific phrases** for the system to understand reliably.
- Limited support for some **languages** (e.g. Kazakh).
- **Privacy** concerns — devices are always listening; voice recordings may be stored.
- Needs a lot of **processing power** / an Internet connection; not suitable in quiet places (library) or noisy ones.

blocks.content: An interface that **recognises movements of the user's body** — hands, fingers, head, eyes or whole body — and interprets them as commands. Input comes from **touchscreens**, **cameras** and **motion / depth sensors**. Examples: swipe and pinch-to-zoom on a phone, **Xbox Kinect**, VR hand controllers, smart TV hand gestures, car controls that change volume with a twirl of the finger.

blocks.title: Types of gesture input
rows: Swipe, pinch to zoom, two-finger scroll
Waving a hand to skip a song, Kinect games
Shaking a phone to undo; tilting to steer in a game
Selecting an item by looking at it in VR

items.title: Advantages of a GRI
items.content:
- **Natural and intuitive** — gestures are like real-world movements; easy for children.
- **No physical contact** needed (for camera-based systems) — **hygienic** in hospitals, kitchens, public kiosks.
- Useful for people who **cannot use a keyboard or mouse**.
- Allows **immersive** interaction in games, VR and AR.
- Fast for simple commands; frees the hands from holding a device.

items.title: Disadvantages of a GRI
items.content:
- Gestures may be **misinterpreted** or made **accidentally** (unintended commands).
- Users must **learn and remember** the gestures; gestures differ between systems and **cultures**.
- Only a **limited number** of commands can be given by gestures.
- **Tiring** for long periods ("gorilla arm").
- Needs **expensive sensors / cameras**; affected by **lighting** and space; less **precise** than a mouse.
- Not suitable for users with some physical disabilities.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a command line interface. [2]**
Advantage: an expert can work **faster** because one command can do a complex task / it uses **less memory** (1). Disadvantage: the user must **remember the commands and syntax**, so it is hard to learn (1).

**Q: Compare a GUI and a CLI. [2]**
A GUI is **easier to learn** because users select icons and menus, **whereas** a CLI requires users to **remember commands** (1). A GUI uses **more memory and processing power**, **whereas** a CLI uses **few resources** (1).

**Q: Write one disadvantage of each of the following user interfaces. [2]**
*Natural language:* language is **ambiguous**, so the system may **misinterpret** the user's request / problems with accents and noise (1).
*Gesture recognition:* gestures may be **misread or made by accident**, causing unintended commands / users must learn the gestures (1).

**Q: Explain why a gesture recognition interface is suitable for a surgeon. [2]**
The surgeon can control the computer **without touching it** (1), so their hands **stay sterile** during the operation (1).

- Saying a CLI is "bad" or "old" — it is **faster and more powerful for experts**.
- Writing "a GUI is easy" without saying **why** (icons, recognition instead of recall, no commands to remember).
- Confusing a **natural language interface** with a **CLI** — typing ordinary sentences to a chatbot is NLI; typing exact commands is CLI.
- Forgetting that a touchscreen GUI uses **gestures** (swipe, pinch), so phones combine GUI and GRI.
- Giving the same point twice (e.g. "easy to use" and "user-friendly").
